title: The broad reach and inaccuracy of men's health information on social media: analysis of TikTok and Instagram
screen_reason: QUALITY/accuracy-scale study reported as MEANS ONLY. Accuracy of the 234 sampled TikTok posts (educational posts only) was scored on a 1-5 'misinformation index' (1 = complete lack of accurate information, 5 = complete lack of inaccurate information) and is reported solely as means with SDs - overall 2.6 +/- 1.7; physicians 4.2 +/- 1.2 vs non-physicians 2.3 +/- 1.6; by topic 1.5 (semen retention) to 5.0 (vasectomy). No share of posts is ever classified as false, inaccurate or misinformation, and no counts by score are given, so no share is derivable under R8. The instructions are explicit on both points: a Likert accuracy scale reported only as a mean is not a share and yields no row, and scale-means-only studies are excluded. No accuracy assessment at all was performed on Instagram. The remaining percentages in the paper (creator type, content category, engagement, impressions) describe who posts and what people watched, never whether it was true.
missed_or_uncertain: Numbers examined and rejected, with reasons: (a) 'Across all men's health topics on TT, educational posts had a mean misinformation index score of 2.6 +/- 1.7' and Table 4's per-topic means (testosterone 2.3, ED 2.8, male infertility 3.0, semen retention 1.5, Peyronie's 3.6, vasectomy 5.0) - a 1-5 accuracy scale reported as means only; no share of posts falls above or below any threshold, and no per-score counts are given, so nothing is derivable. If the authors had reported the number of posts scoring below 5 this would have been an extractable CONTENT share, since the scale anchors are explicitly about presence of inaccurate information and scoring was expert (fellowship-trained urologist) verification against the medical literature. (b) Semen retention accounted for 1,216,074,000 of 2,312,407,100 TikTok impressions (52.6%) and 1,077,000 of 3,107,300 Instagram posts (34.7%), and the authors state semen retention is 'not supported by current literature' with the lowest accuracy score (1.5). This is the closest thing in the paper to an EXPOSURE share, but it is the share of views on a TOPIC, not the share of views of content classified as false: the topic label is not a veracity coding, individual posts on it averaged 1.5 rather than a uniform 1, and treating 52.6% as 'misinformation exposure' would import the reviewer's judgement, not the paper's. Not extracted; flagged here in case an adjudicator disagrees. (c) Physician posts 10.3% (24/234) of TikTok and 12.9% (31/240) of Instagram posts; healthcare workers 15.5% and 17.3%; educational content 50.9% and 32.5%; verified accounts 3.0% and 0.8% - creator and content-type shares with no veracity component. (d) Engagement totals (47,142,691 likes; 679,443 comments; 1,338,473 shares; 36,302,656 followers) and their physician/non-physician splits - no misinformation denominator. (e) Intro figures cited from elsewhere (72% of US adults using social media, 50% of parents verifying with doctors) - barred by R8 as figures the paper cites from other sources.

rob.design: Cross-sectional social-media content analysis at a single time point. Six men's health topics chosen by author consensus (an acknowledged selection bias; core topics such as premature ejaculation were omitted while semen retention, 'not considered a core men's health issue', was included). For each topic the top ten associated hashtags were searched on TikTok and Instagram to total impressions (TikTok views) or post counts (Instagram, which gives no view data). Characterisation sample: the top 40 posts per topic (top 20 posts x top 2 hashtags), giving 234 TikTok posts (only 34 available for Peyronie's disease) and 240 Instagram posts; non-English posts excluded. Two authors (JAA, JMD) reviewed posts for characterisation, a THIRD author adjudicated equivocal cases, but accuracy scoring was done by a SINGLE author (JMD) - the authors themselves flag this as potential bias - so there is no inter-rater reliability statistic for the accuracy measure. Accuracy instrument: a 1-5 'misinformation index' adapted from prior YouTube prostate-cancer work, applied to educational TikTok posts only; no accuracy assessment on Instagram at all (justified by the prevalence of static, low-information posts). Two-sided t-tests, STATA 17. Popularity-ranked sampling means the denominator is a rank-truncated set, not a random sample of platform content.
rob.item6_quote: Each post was reviewed for accuracy and scored to the extent of misinformation on a scale from one to five, based on previously reported methods for characterization of misinformation on prostate cancer on YouTube, which was deemed the misinformation index score [11]. A score of one indicated a complete lack of accurate information (i.e., most inaccurate), whereas a score of five indicated a complete lack of inaccurate information (i.e., most accurate).
rob.item10_quote: Across all men's health topics on TT, educational posts had a mean misinformation index score of 2.6 +/- 1.7. Among educational posts, physician posts were significantly more accurate than non-physician posts (4.2 +/- 1.2 vs 2.3 +/- 1.6, p < 0.001, respectively). [No numerator/denominator share of inaccurate posts is reported anywhere in the paper.]
